lesson_title: Same Mass, Different Weight: You on the Moon
hook_text: Go to the Moon and you lose five sixths of your weight. You do not lose a single gram of mass.
clip_script: Here is a trick question. You stand on a scale and it says 60 kilograms. Is that your weight? Scientifically, no. That is your mass, the amount of stuff you are made of, and it is the same everywhere in the universe. Your weight is how hard a planet pulls you, a force measured in newtons. On Earth each kilogram is pulled with about 9,8 newtons, so 60 kilograms weighs about 588 newtons. Fly to the Moon, where gravity is about one sixth as strong, and you weigh only about 96 newtons. Same body, same mass, and you could jump six times higher. Gravity treats everything fairly, too. On the airless Moon an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather together, and they landed at the same moment. And astronauts in the space station still have gravity; they float because they are falling around the Earth.
visual_style: A bathroom scale on Earth and the Moon side by side; numbers changing in newtons; astronaut bounding on the Moon; hammer and feather dropping in slow motion; the space station orbiting.
pacing: Trick-question hook, quick maths, then a slow-motion drop and a floating finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work out your weight on Mars.
